Key Fact

All Christians agree that God is the ultimate creator of everything. They disagree about how to interpret the Genesis account — literally (six 24-hour days) or non-literally (metaphorical, compatible with science). The exam often tests these “common and divergent views.”

Christian Beliefs About the Afterlife

Christians believe that physical death is not the end. What happens after death is a central part of Christian faith, and different Christians hold different views about the details.

Resurrection and Life After Death

Resurrection is the belief that the dead will be raised to new life. Christians believe this because Jesus himself was resurrected three days after his crucifixion. St Paul wrote: “If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile” (1 Corinthians 15:17) — showing that resurrection is absolutely central to Christianity.

Some Christians believe in bodily resurrection — that the physical body will be raised and transformed. Others believe in spiritual resurrection — that the soul lives on in a new spiritual form. Catholics believe the body and soul are reunited at the resurrection on the last day.

Judgement

Christians believe God will judge every person after death. Some Christians distinguish between two types of judgement:

Particular judgement: This happens immediately after a person dies. Their soul is judged by God and sent to heaven, hell or (in Catholic belief) purgatory.

Final (Last) judgement: At the end of time, Jesus will return and judge all people — both the living and the dead. This is described in Matthew 25:31–46, the parable of the sheep and the goats, where those who helped others are welcomed into God’s kingdom and those who did not are sent away.

Heaven and Hell

Heaven is understood as a state of eternal happiness and peace in the presence of God. It is the ultimate reward for those who have lived according to God’s will. Jesus told the criminal crucified beside him: “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43).

Hell is understood as eternal separation from God. Some Christians believe hell is a literal place of fire and torment. Others interpret it as the absence of God’s love and presence — a spiritual suffering rather than a physical one. Some liberal Christians question whether a loving God would condemn anyone to eternal suffering.

Key Fact

Beliefs about the afterlife influence how Christians live. Because they believe in judgement, they try to live morally, follow Jesus’s teachings, help others and avoid sin. The hope of heaven brings comfort in times of suffering, and the possibility of hell motivates them to stay on the right path.

Catholics also believe in purgatory — a state of purification after death where souls are cleansed of their sins before entering heaven. This is not a Protestant belief. Catholics pray for the dead, asking God to release souls from purgatory sooner.

title: Mission, Evangelism and World Poverty
content_html:
The Place of Mission and Evangelism

Mission is at the heart of Christianity. Christians believe they have a duty to share the good news about Jesus Christ with non-believers. This calling comes directly from the words of Jesus himself. Evangelism is one of the main ways this mission is carried out — through public preaching, personal conversations, and organised events that invite people to learn about the Christian faith.

Key Fact

Mission means “sent out” — it refers to the duty of Christians to go into the world and spread their faith. Evangelism is the practice of spreading the Christian gospel by public preaching or personal witness.

The Great Commission

The Great Commission is the instruction Jesus gave to his disciples after his resurrection. It is recorded in Matthew 28:16–20. Jesus told his eleven disciples: “Go, then, to all peoples everywhere and make them my disciples: baptise them in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and teach them to obey everything I have commanded you.”

This passage is significant for three reasons. First, Jesus commands his followers to make disciples of all nations — not just believers, but people who actively follow his teachings. Second, he instructs them to baptise new converts, showing that baptism has been central to the Church from the very beginning. Third, he tells them to teach obedience to his commandments, meaning the disciples must pass on Jesus’ moral and spiritual teachings.

Jesus also said: “Come, follow me… and I will send you out to fish for people” (Matthew 4:19). At Pentecost, the Holy Spirit gave the disciples the gifts and courage they needed to carry out this mission.

Christians spread their faith in several ways. They talk to friends, family, and colleagues about their beliefs. Some become missionaries, travelling to other countries to preach and carry out humanitarian work among the poor and disadvantaged. Others use social media, television channels like God TV, and Christian radio to reach wider audiences. Many churches invite people to attend events, services, or informal gatherings as a first step towards faith.

Church Growth

The Church is growing rapidly in South America, Africa, and Asia, though growth has slowed in the USA, Europe, and the Middle East. Worldwide, around 80,000 people become Christians each day, and over 500 new churches begin. The Church’s mission is to make new disciples, not just new believers — this means evangelism should be followed by training new converts in the way of following Jesus and spreading the faith.

The Alpha Course — started as a way to help church members understand the basics of the Christian faith. It is now used as an introduction for anyone interested in learning about Christianity. Described as “an opportunity to explore the meaning of life,” Alpha courses are held in homes, workplaces, universities, prisons, and churches.

The Church Army — helps people find faith and works with vulnerable and marginalised people in society, bringing them into the Church.

Christ for all Nations (CfaN) — an international evangelism organisation that holds large-scale events to spread the Christian gospel worldwide.

Fresh Expressions of Church — new and creative forms of church designed to engage with people who might not otherwise think of attending a traditional church service.

The Church’s Response to World Poverty

Christians believe they have a responsibility to help those living in poverty because Jesus taught that this was important. The causes of world poverty include debt, natural disasters, disease, conflict, unfair trade, lack of education, inadequate healthcare, and corrupt leaders. Three major Christian charities work to address these causes.

Key Fact

Three key Christian charities that respond to world poverty are CAFOD, Tearfund, and Christian Aid. Each provides both emergency relief and long-term development support, motivated by Jesus’ teachings about caring for the poor.

CAFOD (Catholic Agency for Overseas Development) works to train and support communities to work their way out of poverty. It provides short-term aid such as food, water, and shelter during disasters. CAFOD also campaigns with the government and encourages Catholic churches and schools to donate money and pray for those in need.

Tearfund works with churches worldwide to lift people out of poverty. It supplies emergency aid after natural disasters and provides long-term aid to help communities become more self-reliant. Tearfund is supported by fundraising and prayer from churches.

Christian Aid supports projects to encourage sustainable development. It provides emergency relief such as food, water, shelter, and sanitation. Christian Aid also campaigns to end poverty and global warming, and works to encourage fair trade.

Biblical Teachings on Poverty

Jesus’ teachings provide the motivation for Christian responses to world poverty. Jesus once told a rich man to sell everything and give to the poor, saying: “It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for someone who is rich to enter the Kingdom of God.” The Parable of the Rich Man and Lazarus tells of a wealthy man who ends up in hell for ignoring a beggar at his gate.

The Bible also teaches: “Faith without action is dead” (James 2:26), meaning Christians must put their beliefs into practical action. In 1 John 3:17–18, it says: “If anyone has material possessions and sees a brother or sister in need but has no pity on them, how can the love of God be in that person? Dear children, let us not love with words or speech but with actions and truth.”

Key Fact

The Parable of the Sheep and Goats (Matthew 25) teaches that those who help the hungry, thirsty, and needy are serving God himself: “Whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers and sisters of mine, you did for me.”

title: Pilgrimage and Celebrations
content_html:
What Is Pilgrimage?

A pilgrimage is a journey to a place of special religious significance. Christians go on pilgrimages to deepen their faith, seek healing, do penance, experience God in a special way, or feel a connection to important events in Christian history. Some Christians believe that visiting a sacred place brings them closer to God. Others see the journey itself as a spiritual act — a time for prayer, reflection and personal growth.

Not all Christians agree that pilgrimage is necessary. Some argue that God is everywhere and can be worshipped anywhere. Others believe the money spent on travel could be better used to help the poor. However, many Christians value pilgrimage as a powerful expression of faith that has been practised since the earliest centuries of Christianity.

Key Fact

You need to know two contrasting examples of Christian pilgrimage: Lourdes (Roman Catholic, focus on healing) and Iona (ecumenical, focus on community and simplicity). Be ready to explain why Christians visit each and how they differ.

Lourdes

Lourdes is a town in south-west France. In 1858, a 14-year-old girl named Bernadette Soubirous reported 18 visions of the Virgin Mary in a grotto near the river. During one vision, Mary told Bernadette to dig in the ground, and a spring of water appeared. This water is believed by many Catholics to have miraculous healing properties.

Today, around six million pilgrims visit Lourdes each year, making it one of the most visited Christian pilgrimage sites in the world. Pilgrims bathe in or drink the spring water, hoping for physical or spiritual healing. The site includes the Grotto of Massabielle (where the visions occurred), the Basilica of the Immaculate Conception, and hospitals and care facilities for the sick. Over 70 miraculous cures have been officially recognised by the Catholic Church.

Christians visit Lourdes to seek physical healing by bathing in or drinking the spring water. They also go to seek spiritual renewal and forgiveness through prayer and confession. Many go to pray for others who are sick, to feel closer to God in a place associated with the Virgin Mary, or to serve as volunteers caring for the sick and disabled. The sense of community at Lourdes — with millions of believers gathering together — strengthens faith and provides support for those who are suffering.

Iona

Iona is a small island off the west coast of Scotland. In 563 CE, an Irish monk named St Columba founded a monastery there, which became a centre for spreading Christianity across Scotland and northern England. Today, the Iona Community is an ecumenical Christian community that welcomes people of all denominations and none.

Pilgrims visit Iona for its simplicity, peace and sense of spiritual renewal. The community emphasises justice, peace and the integrity of creation. Visitors share in communal worship, manual work and discussion. Unlike Lourdes, Iona does not focus on miracles or healing — instead, it offers a retreat from modern life and an opportunity to live in a simple, prayerful community.

Christmas

Christmas celebrates the Incarnation — the belief that God became human in the person of Jesus Christ. Christians celebrate Christmas on 25 December (though Orthodox Christians celebrate on 7 January). The festival recalls the birth of Jesus in Bethlehem, as described in the Gospels of Matthew and Luke.

Christmas is important because it marks the moment God entered the world as a human being to save humanity from sin. The angel told the shepherds, “Today in the town of David a Saviour has been born to you; he is the Messiah, the Lord” (Luke 2:11). Christians celebrate through special church services (including Midnight Mass and carol services), nativity plays, gift-giving (symbolising the gifts of the Magi) and acts of charity.

For Christians in Great Britain today, Christmas remains the most widely celebrated religious festival. It brings families and communities together. Churches hold special services, including Advent services in the weeks leading up to Christmas, Midnight Mass on Christmas Eve, and Christmas Day worship. Many Christians also see it as a time to help those in need — through charity appeals, food drives and volunteering.

Some Christians are concerned that the religious meaning of Christmas has been overshadowed by commercialism and consumerism. They argue that the focus should be on Jesus’s birth and its theological significance, not on shopping and materialism.

Easter

Easter is the most important festival in the Christian calendar. It celebrates the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, three days after his crucifixion. The events of Easter are central to the Christian faith: without the resurrection, there would be no Christianity. St Paul wrote, “If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile” (1 Corinthians 15:17).

Palm Sunday remembers Jesus’s triumphal entry into Jerusalem, when crowds waved palm branches and shouted “Hosanna!” Maundy Thursday recalls the Last Supper, when Jesus washed his disciples’ feet and shared bread and wine. Good Friday marks the crucifixion and death of Jesus — many churches hold sombre services, and some Christians fast or walk the Stations of the Cross. Easter Sunday celebrates the resurrection — churches hold joyful services with hymns, flowers and the lighting of the Paschal candle.

Key Fact

Easter is the most important Christian festival because it celebrates the resurrection — the foundation of the entire Christian faith. St Paul wrote, “If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile” (1 Corinthians 15:17). Without the resurrection, Christians believe there would be no hope of salvation or eternal life.

title: Incarnation and Redemption
content_html:
The Incarnation: God Becomes Human

The incarnation is one of the most distinctive and central claims of Catholic Christianity: the eternal Son of God — the second person of the Trinity — entered human history as a real human being. The word comes from the Latin in carne, meaning ‘in the flesh.’ The Gospel of John expresses it directly: “The Word became flesh and made his dwelling among us” (John 1:14). For Catholics, this is not a metaphor — Jesus of Nazareth, born of Mary in first-century Palestine, was and is fully God and fully human at the same time.

The precise phrase used by Catholic theology is that Jesus has “two natures in one person” — the divine nature and the human nature united in the single person of Christ. This was formally defined at the Council of Chalcedon (451 CE). The two natures are “without confusion, without change, without division, without separation.” This means Jesus genuinely experienced human life: he was born, he grew, he felt hunger, friendship, grief and fear. Yet he also demonstrated divine knowledge, authority and power. For Catholics, both aspects are equally real and equally important.

The Incarnation is grounded in multiple scriptural sources. The opening of John’s Gospel identifies Jesus as the eternal Logos (Word) who “was with God” and “was God” (John 1:1) before becoming flesh. Matthew and Luke record the virginal conception of Jesus — Mary conceives through the Holy Spirit, not through human agency (Matthew 1:18–25, Luke 1:26–38). Paul’s letters in the New Testament reflect an early high Christology: in Philippians 2:6–8, he describes how Christ “being in very nature God, did not consider equality with God something to be used to his own advantage; rather, he made himself nothing by taking the very nature of a servant, being made in human likeness.”

The Nicene Creed, recited at every Catholic Mass, captures this scriptural teaching in its definitive formula: “For us and for our salvation he came down from heaven: by the power of the Holy Spirit he became incarnate of the Virgin Mary, and was made man.” The phrase “for us and for our salvation” is theologically crucial — the incarnation is not simply a divine visitation but the beginning of the redemptive work of Christ.

The Life and Ministry of Jesus

Catholics understand the entire life of Jesus, not just his death, as redemptively significant. His miracles — healing the sick, feeding the hungry, raising the dead — are signs of the coming Kingdom of God. His teachings, especially the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5–7), articulate the values of God’s kingdom: mercy, peacemaking, justice, purity of heart. His relationships — with women, with the poor, with tax collectors and sinners — enact the inclusive love of God. For Catholics, imitating Jesus in daily life is inseparable from being saved by him.

Key Fact

The four key events through which Catholics understand redemption: (1) the life of Jesus — his teachings and miracles reveal God’s kingdom; (2) the death of Jesus on the cross — atoning sacrifice for human sin; (3) the resurrection — Jesus rises from the dead on the third day, defeating sin and death; (4) the ascension — Jesus returns to the Father, sending the Holy Spirit to be with the Church.

The Death of Jesus: Atonement and Sacrifice

The death of Jesus on the cross is understood by Catholics as an act of atonement — a sacrifice that restores the broken relationship between humanity and God caused by sin. Paul writes: “God demonstrates his own love for us in this: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). The sacrifice of Jesus is understood as a free act of love that meets the demands of divine justice while expressing divine mercy. Catholics believe this sacrifice is made present at every Mass through the Eucharist — one of the reasons the Mass holds such central importance in Catholic life.

Different theological traditions within Christianity have developed different models of atonement. Substitutionary atonement, emphasised in some Protestant traditions, holds that Jesus took the punishment humanity deserved in our place. Catholic theology acknowledges this dimension but tends to give equal weight to the idea of moral exemplar and to the concept of participation: through the death and resurrection of Christ, believers are drawn into a new relationship with God. The cross is not only a transaction but a revelation of God’s love.

Resurrection and Ascension

The resurrection of Jesus is the cornerstone of Catholic faith. Paul states plainly: “If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile; you are still in your sins” (1 Corinthians 15:17). Catholics believe Jesus rose bodily — not as a ghost or merely spiritual presence — and was encountered by his disciples over a period of forty days. The resurrection confirms the truth of everything Jesus taught and promised, and it is the ground of Catholic hope that death is not the final word for any human being.

The ascension follows the resurrection. Jesus returns to the Father (Acts 1:9–11) and sends the Holy Spirit at Pentecost to be with the Church. For Catholics, the ascension does not mean Jesus has abandoned humanity — he remains present through the Eucharist, the Church and the Spirit. The ascension is also the basis of grace: the Holy Spirit poured out at Pentecost enables believers to share in the divine life and empowers them to live as disciples. Salvation, in Catholic understanding, is both an event (achieved on the cross) and an ongoing process (lived out through grace and the sacraments).

All three major Christian traditions teach that salvation is made possible through Jesus Christ, but they emphasise different aspects. Catholic and Orthodox Christianity understand salvation as theosis or divinisation — a gradual transformation of the believer through grace, the sacraments and a life of virtue, drawing the person into ever-deeper union with God. This is an ongoing process, not a single moment of decision.

Many Protestant traditions, particularly those in the evangelical and Reformed stream, emphasise justification by faith — that a person is declared righteous before God through faith in Christ alone, not through works or sacraments. Catholic theology accepts justification by faith but insists that genuine faith naturally produces good works, and that the sacraments are the means through which grace is communicated. The Council of Trent (1545–1563) clarified the Catholic position in response to the Protestant Reformation. In practice, all traditions agree that the death and resurrection of Jesus are the foundation of salvation.

Key Fact

Grace is God’s free gift to humanity made possible through the life, death and resurrection of Jesus. In Catholic teaching, grace is communicated primarily through the seven sacraments — especially baptism (which removes original sin and begins the life of grace) and the Eucharist (which nourishes and sustains it). Grace enables the believer to do what would be impossible by human effort alone: to love as God loves, to forgive as God forgives.

title: Mission, Evangelism and Catholic Charities
content_html:
What Is Mission?

Mission is the task given by the risen Jesus to his followers: “Go and make disciples of all nations, baptising them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and teaching them to obey everything I have commanded you” (Matthew 28:19–20). This command, known as the Great Commission, is foundational to Catholic identity. The Catholic Church understands itself as a missionary Church — not in the sense of imposing its beliefs on others, but in the sense that it has something of great importance to offer: the Good News of God’s love and the invitation to share in the life of Christ.

Evangelism (or evangelisation) is the process of sharing the Good News. For Catholics today in Britain, evangelism takes many forms: inviting friends and neighbours to Mass, running faith exploration courses (such as RCIA — the Rite of Christian Initiation of Adults), speaking openly about faith in workplaces and schools, and engaging in dialogue with people of other faiths. Pope Francis has consistently urged Catholics to be a “missionary Church” — one that reaches out rather than waiting for people to come to it.

Key Fact

The Great Commission (Matthew 28:19–20): Jesus commands his disciples to “go and make disciples of all nations, baptising them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” This is the foundation of Catholic mission: the Gospel is not private property but a gift to be shared with everyone. Catholics in Britain today engage in evangelism through faith courses, parish outreach and community service.

The Society of Saint Vincent de Paul (SVP)

The Society of Saint Vincent de Paul (SVP) was founded in Paris in 1833 by a group of young Catholic university students led by Frédéric Ozanam. It is named after St Vincent de Paul (1581–1660), a French priest who dedicated his life to the service of the poor and who reformed the training of priests and the care of the sick and orphaned in seventeenth-century France.

The SVP is an international lay organisation operating in 153 countries. Its members — called Vincentians — visit people in their homes, hospitals and care homes, offer practical help (food parcels, clothing, furniture), befriend the lonely and isolated, and run projects for the homeless, the unemployed and those in financial difficulty. The SVP operates through local parish conferences (groups), making it one of the most locally embedded Catholic charitable organisations in Britain. Its motto is “Serviens in Spe” — “Serving in Hope.”

What distinguishes the SVP from purely secular charities is its emphasis on the personal relationship: Vincentians do not simply deliver goods, they sit with the people they serve, treating each person as Christ. The theological grounding is Matthew 25:40: “Whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers and sisters of mine, you did for me.” In a Catholic parish in Liverpool, for example, the local SVP conference might visit elderly parishioners who cannot attend Mass, bring Holy Communion to the housebound, run a lunch club for the lonely, and collect food for a local food bank.

Pax Christi (Latin: “Peace of Christ”) is an international Catholic peace movement founded in 1945, initially as a movement of Franco-German reconciliation after the Second World War. It now works in over forty countries, campaigning for disarmament (including opposition to nuclear weapons), challenging militarism, and promoting reconciliation between enemies as a concrete expression of the Gospel.

Pax Christi’s theological foundation is the Beatitude “Blessed are the peacemakers” (Matthew 5:9) and the Catholic commitment to the “just war” tradition alongside its increasingly strong pacifist strand. In Britain, Pax Christi UK campaigns against the Trident nuclear weapons programme, works with schools on peace education, and runs interfaith peace-building initiatives. The organisation sees disarmament not as political preference but as a moral requirement flowing from the sanctity of human life and the command to love one’s enemy (Matthew 5:44).

The Corrymeela Community is an ecumenical Christian reconciliation community in Northern Ireland, founded in 1965 by Ray Davey — a Presbyterian minister who had been a prisoner of war and had witnessed the destruction of Dresden. Located at a residential centre on the Antrim coast, Corrymeela brings together Catholics and Protestants divided by the violence of the Troubles, young people from different communities, and families affected by conflict, to work together on healing and understanding.

Corrymeela is notable for being explicitly Christian but ecumenical — it does not belong to one denomination. Its work is grounded in the conviction that the Gospel calls all Christians to reconciliation, drawing on Paul’s letter to the Corinthians: “All this is from God, who reconciled us to himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation” (2 Corinthians 5:18). While primarily Protestant in origin, the GCSE specification names Corrymeela alongside Pax Christi as an example of Catholic-engaged peace-building, because it works across the Catholic-Protestant divide and many Catholics participate in its work.

Catholics in Great Britain: Mission Today

There are approximately five million Catholics in England and Wales, making Catholicism the largest single Christian denomination. Catholics in Britain today engage in mission in a context very different from earlier centuries: a secular, pluralist society in which faith is often treated as a private matter. The challenge of Catholic mission in Britain is therefore not primarily overseas but local: how to share the Gospel with a society that is largely unchurched, and how to demonstrate the relevance of Catholic teaching and practice to contemporary life.

This local mission takes many forms. Westminster Cathedral in London hosts regular public events, concerts, lectures and open days to engage people who might not otherwise encounter Catholicism. Individual parishes run Alpha and RCIA courses for people exploring the faith. The Catholic Bishops’ Conference of England and Wales speaks publicly on issues of justice, education and family life, acting as a public voice for Catholic Social Teaching in national debate. For Catholics, none of this is separate from the central command: “Love the Lord your God… and love your neighbour as yourself” (Matthew 22:37–39).

Key Fact

SVP: international lay organisation visiting and serving the poor person-to-person in 153 countries, grounded in Matthew 25:40 (“Whatever you did for the least…”). Pax Christi: international Catholic peace movement working for disarmament and nonviolent conflict resolution, grounded in the Beatitude (Matthew 5:9). Corrymeela: ecumenical reconciliation community in Northern Ireland, bringing Catholics and Protestants together, grounded in 2 Corinthians 5:18.

title: Pilgrimage and the Funeral Rite
content_html:
What Is Pilgrimage?

Pilgrimage is a journey made to a sacred place for religious purposes. It is one of the oldest expressions of religious devotion across many traditions, and it plays a significant role in Catholic Christianity. Catholics go on pilgrimage to be closer to God, to seek healing or forgiveness, to pray for others, to deepen their faith, or to fulfil a vow. The physical act of journeying — leaving home, enduring discomfort, travelling with other believers — is understood as mirroring the spiritual journey of the Christian life itself: a movement toward God.

Three major sites draw Catholic pilgrims: Lourdes in France, Walsingham in Norfolk, and the Holy Land. Rome — with St Peter’s Basilica, the catacombs and the Vatican — is also a major destination for Catholic pilgrims, especially in Jubilee years.

Key Fact

Lourdes: pilgrims visit seeking healing (physical and spiritual), bathing in the spring water near the Grotto de Massabielle where Mary appeared to Bernadette. Over six million visitors a year, including many sick and disabled people brought by Catholic volunteer groups. Walsingham: pilgrims walk the “Holy Mile” barefoot as an act of devotion and visit the Shrine of Our Lady of Walsingham.

Lourdes: Healing and Community

Lourdes in southern France became a major pilgrimage site following 1858, when a fourteen-year-old girl called Bernadette Soubirous reported eighteen apparitions of the Virgin Mary at a grotto near the town. Bernadette was told to drink from a spring at the grotto that she initially could not find — when she scratched the ground, water appeared. Since then, the spring has been associated with numerous reported miraculous healings, some of which have been subjected to medical investigation by the Bureau des Constatations Médicales (the Medical Bureau of Lourdes). The Church has officially recognised 70 miracles at Lourdes after rigorous investigation.

For Catholics, Lourdes is not only about physical healing. Many pilgrims who are not physically cured report a deep spiritual renewal — a sense of God’s presence, renewed faith, and the experience of community with other pilgrims. The great candlelit processions, the immersion in the baths, the torchlight rosary procession each evening — all create a profound atmosphere of prayer. British Catholic organisations such as HCPT (Handicapped Children’s Pilgrimage Trust) take thousands of children with disabilities to Lourdes every year, expressing the Catholic conviction that the sick and vulnerable hold a special place in the heart of God.

Walsingham: England's Nazareth

Walsingham in Norfolk has been a place of Christian pilgrimage since 1061, when a noblewoman called Richeldis de Faverches reportedly received a vision of Mary and was asked to build a replica of the Holy House of Nazareth. The original Shrine of Our Lady of Walsingham was destroyed during the Reformation, but pilgrimage resumed in the twentieth century. Today, both a Catholic and an Anglican shrine stand in Walsingham, drawing pilgrims from across Britain. Walsingham is often called “England’s Nazareth” — a way of bringing the Holy Land spiritually close to British Catholics.

Pilgrims to Walsingham traditionally walk the final mile (the “Holy Mile”) barefoot as a penitential act, following the example of medieval pilgrims and countless generations of believers. The Slipper Chapel, where pilgrims removed their shoes before walking the final stretch, is the Catholic national shrine of England.

Catholic and Orthodox Christians strongly value pilgrimage. Orthodox pilgrims journey to Mount Athos, Jerusalem, the monasteries of Meteora and to numerous local shrines. The physical journey is understood as spiritually formative — a way of honouring sacred places and seeking God’s grace in a particular location.

Most Protestant Christians are more cautious about pilgrimage, particularly to Marian shrines. Reformers such as Martin Luther criticised pilgrimage as a “work” that could not earn salvation and argued that God’s presence is not tied to physical locations. Protestants generally hold that a believer can encounter God anywhere through prayer and scripture, and that special sacred places are not necessary. Some evangelical Christians do travel to the Holy Land for educational and devotional purposes, but regard it as tourism rather than a meritorious religious act. This contrast between Catholic and Protestant views on pilgrimage is a significant mark-scheme point.

The Catholic Funeral Rite

The Catholic funeral rite is not a farewell alone — it is a liturgical celebration of faith in the resurrection. The Catholic Church’s Order of Christian Funerals describes three key moments: the Vigil (a prayer service held the night before burial), the Funeral Mass (the Requiem Mass), and the Rite of Committal (at the graveside or crematorium). Together these express the Catholic belief that the person who has died is not lost but has passed into God’s care.

The Requiem Mass is at the centre of the Catholic funeral rite. The word “requiem” comes from the Latin for “rest” — the opening prayer asks God to grant the deceased eternal rest. The white or gold vestments worn by the priest (rather than black) reflect the resurrection hope at the heart of Catholic funerals. The body of the deceased is treated with great respect: because Catholics believe in the resurrection of the body, the body of a dead person is regarded as a temple of the Holy Spirit that will one day be raised.

For most of its history, the Catholic Church preferred burial over cremation because burial was seen as more clearly symbolising the resurrection of the body and following the example of Jesus, who was buried in a tomb. Cremation was permitted by the Church from 1963 onwards, provided it is not chosen for reasons that deny the resurrection. Today most Catholics in Britain are cremated. However, the Church continues to prefer that the body be present at the Requiem Mass before cremation, and that the ashes be buried or interred in a sacred place rather than scattered.

Key Fact

The Requiem Mass affirms the resurrection of the body: the priest wears white or gold (not black), and the liturgy includes the words “I am the resurrection and the life” (John 11:25) and prayers for the soul’s purification in purgatory. The body is treated reverently as a temple of the Holy Spirit that will be raised. Catholics who die are commended to God’s mercy at every Requiem.

title: The Nature of God & the Trinity
content_html:
The Nature of God

Christians are monotheistic — they believe in one God who created and sustains everything. Although God is called “Father,” Christians do not believe God has a physical body or a gender. God is a spirit, beyond human understanding, and is considered holy — completely pure, set apart and worthy of worship.

The Nicene Creed, recited by Christians worldwide, opens with the words: “We believe in One God.” Christians believe this one God has several key qualities that together make God perfect. Three of these qualities are central to the AQA specification: God as omnipotent, God as loving (benevolent), and God as just.

God as Omnipotent

Omnipotent means all-powerful. Christians believe God has unlimited power and authority — nothing is beyond what God can do. God demonstrated this power by creating the entire universe from nothing and continues to sustain all life.

Key Fact

“Nothing is impossible with God.” (Luke 1:37) — These words were spoken by the Angel Gabriel to the Virgin Mary. Christians use this verse to show that God’s power has absolutely no limits.

Belief in God’s omnipotence influences Christians in several ways. When they see the complexity of nature, they see evidence of a powerful creator. It also means they trust that God can perform miracles, and it gives them confidence when they pray that God has the power to answer.

God as Loving (Benevolent)

Benevolent means all-loving and all-good. Christians believe God loves every human being unconditionally. God created humans out of love and wants to share that love with all creation.

Key Fact

“God so loved the world that he gave his one and only Son, that whoever believes in him shall not perish but have eternal life.” (John 3:16) — Christians see sending Jesus as the greatest act of God’s love.

This belief helps Christians feel valued and gives them a purpose — to share God’s love with others through kindness, charity and forgiveness. Because God is all-loving, Christians believe God forgives those who are truly sorry for their sins.

God as Just

Christians believe God is a just (fair) judge of all humanity. Because God is all-powerful and all-loving, God is the perfect giver of justice. This means God will never support injustice, oppression, prejudice or cruelty.

“God is just: He will pay back trouble to those who trouble you.” (2 Thessalonians 1:6) — This teaches Christians that God sees all actions and will judge everyone fairly. No wrongdoing will go unnoticed. Because of this, Christians are motivated to fight against injustice wherever they encounter it.

The Problem of Evil and Suffering

If God is omnipotent, loving and just, why does evil and suffering exist? This is called the problem of evil, and it is one of the biggest challenges to Christian belief.

The problem can be stated simply: if God is loving, he would want to stop suffering; if God is powerful, he could stop suffering; if God is just, he would not allow injustice. Yet suffering clearly exists. The philosopher David Hume called this the “inconsistent triad” — the three ideas seem to contradict each other.

Christians distinguish between two types of evil. Moral evil is caused by human actions — murder, theft, war and cruelty. Natural evil is caused by the natural world — earthquakes, disease, floods and famine.

Free will: God gave humans the freedom to choose how to live. Some choose to do wrong, causing moral evil. Christians argue that genuine free will is better than being puppets, even if some misuse it.

Life as a test: Some Christians believe suffering tests faith. The story of Job shows that God allows suffering to test whether people remain faithful — and rewards those who do.

Part of God’s plan: Humans cannot fully understand God’s reasons. “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you” (Jeremiah 1:5) suggests God has a purpose for every person, even if suffering seems unfair.

The Devil: Some Christians believe Satan tempts people into sin. Evil is caused by the Devil, not by God — though this raises the question of why God allows the Devil to operate.

The Oneness of God and the Trinity

Although Christians believe in one God, they understand God as existing in three persons: Father, Son (Jesus Christ) and Holy Spirit. This is called the Trinity. It does not mean there are three separate gods — the three persons are all fully God, sharing one divine nature.

Key Fact

The Trinity is one God in three persons: the Father (creator and sustainer), the Son (Jesus Christ, who became human to save humanity), and the Holy Spirit (God’s presence active in the world today). All three are equal and eternal.

God the Father is the creator and sustainer of all life. He is the source of all things and the one to whom Christians direct their prayers. Jesus taught his followers to pray “Our Father.”

God the Son is Jesus Christ. Christians believe the Son has always existed with the Father but took human form (the incarnation) to live among people, teach them about God, and die on the cross to save humanity from sin.

God the Holy Spirit is the unseen power of God at work in the world. Christians believe the Holy Spirit guides, comforts and strengthens believers. At Pentecost, the Holy Spirit descended on the disciples as tongues of fire (Acts 2), empowering them to spread the Christian message.

The Nicene Creed affirms the Trinity: “We believe in one God, the Father Almighty… And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God… And in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and Giver of Life.” The Trinity is central to Christian worship — Christians are baptised “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19).

Some Christians find the Trinity difficult to understand. Common analogies include water existing as ice, liquid and steam (three forms, one substance), or the sun giving light, heat and energy. However, these analogies are imperfect — the Trinity is considered a mystery that humans can only partly grasp.

title: Prayer and Popular Piety
content_html:
Prayer as the Raising of Mind and Heart

In Catholic teaching, prayer is defined as “the raising of the mind and heart to God.” This phrase, found in the Catholic Catechism, captures something important about the Catholic understanding of prayer: it is not merely reciting words but an orientation of the whole person — intellect, will and feeling — towards God. Catholics pray alone, with their families, and together as a congregation. Prayer is understood as a relationship, not a transaction — it is how Catholics grow in awareness of God’s presence and respond to his love.

There are two broad kinds of prayer in Catholic practice: formal prayer (set prayers with fixed words, such as the Lord’s Prayer, the Hail Mary, or the Prayer of St Francis) and informal prayer (spontaneous, personal prayer in the believer’s own words). Both are valued in Catholic spirituality, though their relative importance has been debated across Christian traditions.

Key Fact

Catholic prayer is “the raising of the mind and heart to God.” Formal prayer uses fixed, shared texts (the Lord’s Prayer, the Hail Mary) that connect the individual to the wider Church’s tradition. Informal prayer is personal and spontaneous, allowing the believer to express their own joys, sorrows and needs directly to God in their own words.

The Lord's Prayer

The Lord’s Prayer (the “Our Father”) is the prayer taught by Jesus himself when his disciples asked how to pray (Matthew 6:9–13). It is recited at every Mass, at morning and evening prayer, at rosaries and countless other occasions. Because it was given by Jesus, Catholics regard it as the perfect model of prayer: it addresses God as Father, acknowledges his holiness, asks for the coming of his Kingdom, requests daily needs, asks for forgiveness (and commits the pray-er to forgiving others), and seeks protection from evil.

The Lord’s Prayer is also a model of the Catholic understanding of the relationship between formal and informal prayer. Its fixed words carry the meaning and intention of all prayer in condensed form — but those words are not a magic formula. Jesus warns against “babbling on like pagans” (Matthew 6:7) — empty repetition without attention. The Catholic tradition therefore insists that formal prayers must be said with attention, intention and devotion, not merely recited mechanically.

Popular Piety: the Rosary

Popular piety refers to forms of devotion that are not part of the official Mass or Divine Office but are beloved expressions of Catholic faith. The Catholic Catechism describes popular piety as “a true treasure of the People of God.” Two of the most important forms are the Rosary and the Stations of the Cross.

The Rosary is a structured prayer devotion using a string of beads to keep count of prayers. A full Rosary consists of five “decades” — each decade is one Our Father, ten Hail Marys and a Glory Be — while the pray-er meditates on a “mystery” from the lives of Jesus and Mary (Joyful, Sorrowful, Glorious or Luminous Mysteries). Begun in its current form in the fifteenth century and associated with the Dominican religious order, the Rosary is practised by millions of Catholics worldwide. It is a deeply Marian prayer: the Hail Mary (based on Luke 1:28 and Luke 1:42) is at its heart, and it contemplates the life of Jesus through Mary’s perspective as mother and disciple.

Mary holds a uniquely honoured place in Catholic Christianity. Catholics call her the Theotokos (Mother of God — God-bearer), a title affirmed at the Council of Ephesus (431 CE). Catholic teaching holds four distinctive Marian dogmas: the Immaculate Conception (Mary was conceived without original sin), the Perpetual Virginity of Mary, the Divine Motherhood (Theotokos) and the Assumption (Mary was taken body and soul into heaven at the end of her earthly life).

Most Protestant Christians do not practise Marian devotion, arguing that it has no clear New Testament basis and that it risks drawing attention away from Christ himself. Protestants honour Mary as the mother of Jesus and a model of faith and obedience (Luke 1:38: “I am the Lord’s servant”) but do not pray to her or treat her as an intercessor. Eastern Orthodox Christianity shares much Catholic Marian theology but expresses it through icons and the title “Theotokos” rather than through the Rosary, which is a specifically Western Catholic devotion.

Popular Piety: the Stations of the Cross

The Stations of the Cross (the Via Crucis or Way of the Cross) is a devotion in which Catholics move through a series of fourteen or fifteen stations — each representing a scene from Jesus’s passion and death — pausing to pray and reflect at each one. Images of the stations are displayed in virtually every Catholic church worldwide. The devotion is most associated with the season of Lent and Holy Week but is practised year-round.

The Stations originated in the practice of pilgrims walking the Via Dolorosa (the “Way of Grief”) in Jerusalem, following the route Jesus walked to Calvary. The fourteen traditional stations include scenes such as: Jesus is condemned to death; Jesus falls for the first time; Jesus meets his mother Mary; and Jesus is laid in the tomb. A fifteenth station — the Resurrection — has been added in some Catholic communities since the twentieth century, reflecting the insistence that the cross cannot be understood without the resurrection.

Catholic tradition places great weight on formal, liturgical prayer: the Mass, the Divine Office (a daily cycle of prayers said by priests, religious and many lay Catholics), the Rosary. This connects individual prayer to the universal prayer of the Church and to centuries of tradition. The Nicene Creed, the Lord’s Prayer and the Eucharistic Prayer are said in the same form across the world.

Many Protestant traditions, especially charismatic and evangelical ones, emphasise spontaneous, personal prayer as a more authentic expression of a living relationship with God. They may be cautious about repeated formal prayers, pointing to Jesus’s warning about vain repetition (Matthew 6:7). Some Quakers, at the other extreme, reject all fixed forms of prayer and rely entirely on silent waiting and spontaneous Spirit-led speech. Most Christians, whether Catholic or Protestant, value both — the difference is one of emphasis rather than an absolute opposition.

Key Fact

The Rosary: a prayer devotion using beads, combining Our Father, Hail Mary and Glory Be prayers with meditation on the Joyful, Sorrowful, Glorious and Luminous Mysteries — the key events in the lives of Jesus and Mary. The Stations of the Cross: fourteen scenes of Jesus’s passion, displayed in churches and walked prayerfully to enter imaginatively into Christ’s suffering and redemptive love.

title: Sin, Salvation & Atonement
content_html:
What Is Sin?

Sin is any thought or action that goes against God’s will. Christians believe sin damages the relationship between humans and God. Every time a person sins, they move further away from God. Sin can take many forms — lying, stealing, hatred, selfishness, envy and many others.

Christians believe all humans are sinful. Nobody is perfect, and everyone falls short of God’s standards. St Paul wrote: “For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23). This is a problem because God is holy and just — sin cannot exist in God’s presence. Humans therefore need to be saved from the consequences of their sin.

Original Sin

Original sin is the belief that all humans are born with a built-in tendency to do wrong. This idea comes from the story of Adam and Eve in Genesis 3. God placed Adam and Eve in the Garden of Eden and told them not to eat from the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil. The serpent tempted Eve, she ate the fruit, and Adam followed.

Key Fact

Adam and Eve’s disobedience is called the Fall. Christians believe this act of disobedience broke the perfect relationship between God and humanity. As a result, all humans are born with a tendency to sin — this is original sin. It is not a specific sin a person commits, but a condition inherited from the first humans.

Catholic view: Original sin is washed away through the sacrament of baptism. This is one reason Catholics baptise infants — to free the baby from original sin as early as possible. Even after baptism, humans still have a tendency to sin (called concupiscence).

Protestant view: Most Protestants accept the concept of original sin but emphasise that salvation comes through faith in Jesus rather than through sacraments. Some Protestants do not practise infant baptism, believing a person must choose to follow Christ for themselves.

Liberal view: Some liberal Christians see the story of Adam and Eve as a myth that teaches an important truth — humans have a natural tendency to do wrong — rather than a literal historical event. The lesson is the same: humans need God’s help to overcome sin.

What Is Salvation?

Salvation means being saved from sin and its consequences — ultimately, being granted eternal life with God rather than eternal separation from God. Christians believe humans cannot save themselves because all are sinful. They need God’s help.

the specification identifies three means of salvation: law, grace and Spirit. Different Christian traditions emphasise these differently.

Salvation Through Law

Some Christians believe that following God’s laws — the Ten Commandments and the moral teachings of Jesus — is essential for salvation. By obeying God’s commands, a person shows they are devoted to God and deserving of eternal life. Catholics especially emphasise the importance of good works alongside faith — the Epistle of James states: “Faith by itself, if it is not accompanied by action, is dead” (James 2:17).

Salvation Through Grace

Grace is the free, undeserved gift of God’s love. Christians believe God offers salvation not because humans deserve it, but because God loves them. Ephesians 2:8–9 states: “For it is by grace you have been saved, through faith — and this is not from yourselves, it is the gift of God — not by works, so that no one can boast.”

Key Fact

Protestants, especially those in the Reformed tradition, emphasise salvation by grace alone through faith alone. Humans cannot earn salvation by doing good deeds — it is a free gift from God, received through faith in Jesus Christ. Catholics believe both faith and works are necessary — grace enables good works, and both contribute to salvation.

Salvation Through the Holy Spirit

Christians believe the Holy Spirit plays an active role in salvation. The Spirit works within believers to help them recognise their sin, turn towards God, and live a holy life. Charismatic and Pentecostal Christians particularly emphasise the role of the Holy Spirit, believing it gives spiritual gifts such as speaking in tongues, prophecy and healing.

The Holy Spirit guides Christians in daily life, helping them make good decisions and resist temptation. Jesus promised: “The Advocate, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things” (John 14:26). The Spirit also brings comfort in suffering, strengthens faith in difficult times, and empowers Christians to share the gospel with others.

The Role of Christ in Salvation

All Christians agree that Jesus Christ is central to salvation. Without Jesus, humans would remain trapped in sin with no way back to God. Jesus’s death and resurrection made salvation possible.

Atonement

Atonement literally means “at-one-ment” — making God and humanity “at one” again. It is the belief that Jesus’s death on the cross restored the broken relationship between God and humans caused by sin. Through his sacrifice, Jesus took the punishment that humans deserved.

Key Fact

Isaiah 53:5 prophesied the atonement: “He was pierced for our transgressions, he was crushed for our iniquities; the punishment that brought us peace was on him, and by his wounds we are healed.” Christians believe this prophecy was fulfilled by Jesus on the cross.

Substitutionary atonement: Jesus took the place of sinful humans and bore the punishment they deserved. He was a substitute — dying instead of humanity. This view is common among evangelical Protestants.

Satisfaction theory: Human sin offended God’s honour and justice. Only a perfect sacrifice could satisfy God’s justice. Jesus, being sinless, was the only one who could offer this perfect payment. This view is associated with Anselm of Canterbury and is common in Catholic theology.

Moral example: Some liberal Christians see Jesus’s death less as a payment for sin and more as a supreme example of self-sacrificing love. His willingness to die inspires Christians to live selflessly and sacrificially for others.

Regardless of which understanding they hold, all Christians agree that the atonement makes salvation available. Jesus’s sacrifice opened the door for humans to be reconciled with God, forgiven for their sins, and given the promise of eternal life.

title: Sin and Salvation
content_html:
What Is Sin?

In Christianity, sin means any action or thought that goes against God’s will. Sin damages the relationship between humans and God. It can refer to specific wrong actions — such as lying, stealing, or harming others — but it can also describe a deeper state of being separated from God.

Most Christians believe in personal sin — when someone individually chooses to do something wrong, breaking God’s commandments. This is different from the concept of original sin, which affects all of humanity from birth.

Key Fact

Sin separates humans from God. The consequence of sin is believed to be death, but those who are saved receive eternal life.

Original Sin and the Fall

Original sin is the belief that every human is born with a built-in tendency to do wrong. The concept is generally credited to St Augustine and is an important doctrine within the Catholic Church.

According to the Book of Genesis, God placed Adam and Eve in the Garden of Eden and gave them freedom to enjoy everything — except the fruit from the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil. A serpent tempted Eve, and both Adam and Eve ate the forbidden fruit. This act of disobedience is known as “the Fall.”

Eating the fruit made Adam and Eve aware of their own sinful act. They were cast out of paradise, and their disobedience had lasting consequences: separation from God and the introduction of death into the world. Christians believe that this damaged human nature was passed down through all their descendants. As a result, every person is born with an inherited tendency to sin.

Only Mary (Jesus’ mother) and Jesus himself are believed by Catholics to have been born without original sin. The doctrine teaches that because Adam and Eve sinned, all humans need saving — they cannot fix the problem on their own.

Key Fact

“Original sin means the first sin of Adam and Eve. They disobeyed God by eating fruit from the forbidden tree. Humans are now born with a built-in tendency to sin.” — AQA mark scheme summary

What Is Salvation?

Salvation means being saved from sin and its consequences and being granted eternal life with God. Because sin has separated humans from God, salvation is the way back — it enables humans to restore their relationship with God and receive the promise of heaven.

Christians believe that they need saving from sin so they can have a good relationship with God and avoid hell. Most Christians believe that if they put their faith in Jesus, confess their sins and ask for forgiveness, they will be saved.

How Is Salvation Achieved?

the specification identifies several means of salvation: law, grace, and the Holy Spirit. Different Christian traditions place different emphasis on each of these.

Law: In the Old Testament, Jews tried to achieve salvation by following God’s laws, including the Ten Commandments. Christians believe they no longer need to follow all of the Jewish Law because Jesus fulfilled it through his life, death and resurrection. However, many Christians still see living a moral life and doing good works as part of their response to God’s gift of salvation.

Grace: Grace is God’s unconditional love and favour, given freely to humans without them needing to earn it. Many Christians — especially Protestants — believe that salvation comes through grace alone. Jesus coming to save humanity was the ultimate expression of God’s grace. As the Bible teaches: “God so loved the world that He gave his only Son, so that whoever believes in Him shall not perish but have eternal life” (John 3:16).

The Holy Spirit: Many Christians believe that they receive God’s grace through the Holy Spirit, which guides, comforts and strengthens believers in their daily lives. Christians also receive grace through the Bible, prayer and the sacraments.

Salvation by works: Some Christians believe that doing good deeds and following God’s commandments is essential for salvation. The Old Testament emphasises having faith in God and following his rules. The Parable of the Sheep and the Goats (Matthew 25) suggests that people will be judged on their actions — those who helped others will enter heaven.

Salvation by faith (grace): Other Christians, particularly Protestants, believe that salvation comes through faith in Jesus Christ and God’s grace alone — not through good works. They point to passages such as “Whoever believes in me shall have eternal life” (John 6:47). Prayer and asking for forgiveness when we make mistakes are also part of receiving God’s grace.

The Role of Christ in Salvation: Atonement

Atonement is at the heart of Christian belief about salvation. It means restoring the relationship between humans and God through the life, death and resurrection of Jesus. Christians believe that Jesus’ death makes up for the original sin committed by Adam and Eve, and so brings people back to God.

As Son of God, Jesus could easily have avoided being crucified. While he was on the cross, some people shouted to him to use his power to get down. However, he knew his death was needed to restore the relationship between God and believers. This gave all people the opportunity for salvation.

Key Fact

“For since death came through a man, the resurrection of the dead also comes through a man. For as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive.” — 1 Corinthians 15:21–22

Jesus’ resurrection, three days after his death, showed Christians that death had been overcome and that the goodness of Jesus had defeated the power of evil. Atonement removes the effects of sin and allows people to restore their relationship with God. This is only possible because Jesus atoned for the sins of humanity when he died and rose again.

As the Bible says: “If anybody does sin, we have an advocate with the Father — Jesus Christ, the Righteous One. He is the atoning sacrifice for our sins, and not only for ours but also for the sins of the whole world” (1 John 2:1–2).

Atonement is important to Christians because it demonstrates God’s all-loving nature — he died for human beings so they could live with God in peace. It shows the power of good over evil and provides an example for Christians to follow. Atonement offers hope in a world full of suffering. It is remembered in the celebration of Easter and the practice of Holy Communion, and it remains the central message of Christian evangelism.

title: Creation and the Dignity of the Human Person
content_html:
Two Accounts, One Message

The Bible opens with two distinct accounts of creation in Genesis 1 and Genesis 2. Catholic teaching does not require these to be read as competing stories or as a scientific textbook. Instead, the Church understands them as complementary theological accounts that reveal truths about God, the world and human beings. Genesis 1 is a majestic, structured poem in which God creates in six days and rests on the seventh. Genesis 2 is a more intimate narrative focusing on the garden, the first human, and the gift of companionship. Together they form the foundation for the Catholic understanding of creation.

Key Fact

Genesis 1 reveals that God is the source of all existence, that creation is deliberately ordered and good, and that human beings are made in God’s image (imago Dei). Genesis 2 reveals that humanity is formed from the earth yet breathed into life by God — a blend of the material and the spiritual.

Genesis 1 and the Nature of God

In Genesis 1, God creates the world through speech alone: “And God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light.” This emphasises God’s absolute power and sovereignty — nothing exists independently of his will. Each stage of creation is declared “good”, and the whole is declared “very good” (Genesis 1:31). For Catholics, this teaches that the material world is not evil or fallen by nature — it is a gift from a generous Creator. The regular rhythm of six days of work and one day of rest (the Sabbath) models the pattern of human life and later becomes the basis for keeping Sunday holy in Catholic practice.

The pinnacle of Genesis 1 is the creation of humanity on the sixth day: “God created mankind in his own image, in the image of God he created them; male and female he created them” (Genesis 1:27). The concept of imago Dei — being made in God’s image — is central to Catholic anthropology. It means that every human being possesses inherent dignity that cannot be taken away, regardless of their social status, nationality or actions.

Genesis 2 and the Dignity of Human Beings

Genesis 2 presents a more personal creation narrative. The LORD God forms the human from the dust of the ground and “breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living being” (Genesis 2:7). This dual origin — from the earth and from God’s own breath — captures the Catholic understanding of human beings as both physical and spiritual creatures. The body is not a prison for the soul; both together constitute the human person.

The creation of the woman as a partner “suitable for him” (Genesis 2:18) establishes the dignity of both sexes as equally made in God’s image. Catholic teaching, drawing on Genesis 2, insists that neither man nor woman is superior — both reflect the image of God fully. The Catholic Catechism, summarising this teaching, states that human beings are the only creatures God has willed for their own sake.

Christians hold a range of views on the relationship between Genesis and modern science. Creationism (literal six-day creation) is held by some evangelical Protestant Christians, who read Genesis as historical fact. Catholic teaching since at least the papacy of Pius XII has explicitly rejected a rigid literal reading; the Church affirms that the theory of evolution is compatible with belief in God as Creator, provided one upholds that human souls are directly created by God.

Theistic evolution is the position held by most Catholic theologians and by the majority of mainstream Protestant denominations. God is the ultimate cause of the universe’s existence; the scientific account of how life developed is not in competition with the theological account of why it exists. This approach allows Catholics to accept the findings of cosmology and evolutionary biology while affirming that the universe is God’s creation and that every human being has a unique, God-given dignity.

Stewardship of Creation

Genesis 1 calls human beings to “have dominion” over the earth (Genesis 1:28). Catholic teaching interprets this not as a licence to exploit creation but as a call to stewardship — caring for the world as trustees on behalf of God. This position was reinforced by Pope Francis in Laudato Si’ (2015), a major teaching document on care for the environment, which described the earth as “our common home” and argued that the exploitation of natural resources is both an ecological and a moral problem. The document’s argument is grounded directly in the Genesis vision of creation as good and humanity as its responsible guardians.

Catholic communities across Britain today engage in environmental action inspired by this theology: parish eco-groups, fair-trade campaigns, and support for organisations such as CAFOD’s climate justice work all connect the Genesis mandate to present-day responsibility. Orthodox Christianity similarly emphasises creation care, viewing the earth as a sacrament — a means of encountering God. Protestant Christians may emphasise the dominion mandate differently, though many mainstream Protestant denominations now share the Catholic emphasis on responsible stewardship.

A common student error is to interpret “made in God’s image” as a physical resemblance — as if Genesis is claiming God has a body like ours. Catholic theology has consistently interpreted imago Dei as referring to the spiritual and moral capacities that humans share with God: reason, free will, conscience, the capacity for love and relationship. God is not a physical being; the ‘image’ is about what makes humans unique among creatures — their spiritual dimension and moral responsibility. This is a mark-scheme-distinguishing answer.

Key Fact

Imago Dei (Genesis 1:27) means every human being is made in God’s image and therefore possesses inherent dignity and worth. For Catholic teaching this is the foundation of human rights, the condemnation of slavery, abortion, murder and euthanasia, and the call to treat every person as an end in themselves, never merely as a means.

title: Catholic Social Teaching: Loving Our Neighbour
content_html:
Loving Our Neighbour: A Catholic Imperative

When Jesus was asked which commandment was the greatest, he gave two: love God and love your neighbour (Matthew 22:37–39). He illustrated the second with the parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:25–37), making clear that “neighbour” crosses ethnic, religious and social boundaries. For Catholics, the duty to love the neighbour is not optional — it is integral to what it means to follow Christ. This duty is expressed locally (in parish communities), nationally (through Catholic charities and advocacy) and globally (through international agencies such as CAFOD, Trocaire and Missio).

Catholic Social Teaching (CST) is the name given to the set of principles and commitments that the Church has developed for applying the Gospel to the structures of society. It emerged in its modern form in 1891 with Pope Leo XIII’s letter on the condition of workers, and has been developed by every subsequent Pope. Its core principles include the dignity of the human person, the common good, solidarity, subsidiarity (decisions made at the lowest appropriate level), a preferential option for the poor, and care for creation.

Key Fact

Core principles of Catholic Social Teaching: (1) Dignity of the human person — every person is made in God’s image (Genesis 1:27); (2) The common good — the conditions of social life that allow all people to flourish; (3) Preferential option for the poor — the poor and vulnerable have a claim on society’s first resources; (4) Solidarity — we are all members of the human family, responsible for one another.

Gaudium et Spes: Joy and Hope

Gaudium et Spes (“Joy and Hope”) was one of the four constitutions produced by the Second Vatican Council (Vatican II), published in 1965. It is a landmark document that turned the Church’s gaze outward to the world. Paragraph 26 is specifically named in the GCSE specification: it describes the social order as something that must be built on truth, justice and love, and insists that the development of institutions serving the common good is a Christian duty. The document teaches that the joys and griefs of humanity are the joys and griefs of the Church too — the famous opening line is: “The joys and hopes, the griefs and anxieties of the people of this age, especially those who are poor or in any way afflicted, these too are the joys and hopes, the griefs and anxieties of the followers of Christ.”

Before Vatican II, some Catholics understood the Church’s role as primarily sacramental and otherworldly. Gaudium et Spes explicitly rejected this separation: the Church is not above or outside the world but within it, sharing humanity’s struggles and called to transform unjust social structures. This commitment to engaging with the world on questions of poverty, war, human dignity and economic justice remains central to Catholic identity today.

Justice, Peace and Reconciliation

Catholic teaching on justice holds that justice is not merely a legal concept but a moral one rooted in the equal dignity of all human beings. The Catholic Bishops of England and Wales have consistently called for a “just wage” for workers, fair housing, and the protection of asylum seekers — all flowing from the Church’s Social Teaching. The Prophet Amos’s demand “let justice roll on like a river” (Amos 5:24) is often quoted in Catholic social action contexts.

Peace in Catholic teaching is not merely the absence of war but the fruit of justice (a phrase from the Latin opus iustitiae pax — the work of justice is peace). The Church calls Catholics to be peacemakers — echoing the Beatitude “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God” (Matthew 5:9). Reconciliation — the restoration of broken relationships between individuals, communities and nations — is understood as a practical expression of the Gospel command to love one’s enemy (Matthew 5:44).

CAFOD (Catholic Agency for Overseas Development) is the overseas development and relief agency of the Catholic Church in England and Wales. Founded in 1962, it works in more than forty countries, responding to humanitarian crises and supporting long-term development. CAFOD’s work is grounded explicitly in Catholic Social Teaching: its campaigns address climate justice, food security, fair trade and the rights of workers. Each year CAFOD’s fast-day fundraiser engages millions of Catholics in England and Wales in practical solidarity with the world’s poorest communities.

Trocaire is the overseas development agency of the Catholic Church in Ireland (the name means “mercy” in Irish). Like CAFOD, it works to address structural poverty and injustice rather than simply providing emergency relief. Missio is the pontifical mission society of the Catholic Church, supporting the Church’s evangelising work (spreading the faith) alongside practical support for education and healthcare in mission territories. Together these three agencies represent the global reach of Catholic social action: local parish fundraising connects directly to international justice work.

The Gospel Call to Global Solidarity

The Catholic commitment to global solidarity is anchored in the parable of the Sheep and the Goats (Matthew 25:31–46), in which Jesus identifies himself with the hungry, the thirsty, the stranger, the naked, the sick and the prisoner: “Whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers and sisters of mine, you did for me.” For Catholics, serving the poor is not a supplement to faith but an expression of it. Pope Francis’s description of a “Church of the poor” draws directly on this tradition.

At a parish level in Britain today, Catholic Social Teaching shapes a wide range of activities: parish food banks, collections for CAFOD, campaigns against human trafficking (supported by groups like CSAN — Catholic Social Action Network), and parish twinning with communities in the developing world.
