title: Incarnation, Crucifixion & Resurrection
content_html:
The Incarnation

The incarnation is the Christian belief that God became human in the person of Jesus Christ. The word literally means “made flesh.” Christians believe that Jesus was not just a good teacher or prophet — he was God the Son taking on a human body to live among people on Earth.

John 1:14 states: “The Word became flesh and made his dwelling among us.” This connects directly to John 1:1, which says the Word was God. So the Word (God the Son) who created all things became a human being — Jesus of Nazareth. This is one of the most important beliefs in Christianity.

Key Fact

Christians believe Jesus is both fully God and fully human. He was not half-God and half-human, nor God pretending to be human. He experienced everything humans experience — hunger, tiredness, pain, temptation — while also being divine. This is affirmed in the Nicene Creed: “God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God.”

Jesus as the Son of God

Christians call Jesus the Son of God, meaning he has a unique relationship with God the Father. This is not meant literally — God did not have a child in the human sense. Rather, it means Jesus shares God’s divine nature and has existed with the Father for all eternity.

Several events in the Gospels confirm Jesus as the Son of God:

  • At Jesus’s baptism, a voice from heaven said: “This is my Son, whom I love; with him I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17).
  • At the transfiguration, God’s voice again declared: “This is my Son, whom I love. Listen to him!” (Mark 9:7).
  • Jesus performed miracles — healing the sick, calming storms, raising the dead — demonstrating divine power.

The incarnation is significant for several reasons. It shows that God loves humanity enough to become one of us. It means God understands human suffering from personal experience. It also means that Jesus’s teachings carry the full authority of God — when Jesus speaks, God speaks. Finally, it was necessary for salvation: only someone who was both God and human could bridge the gap between a holy God and sinful humanity.

The Crucifixion

The crucifixion refers to the death of Jesus on a Roman cross. Jesus was arrested, tried, and sentenced to death by the Roman governor Pontius Pilate. He was nailed to a cross and died on a Friday, now commemorated as Good Friday.

Christians believe the crucifixion was not simply a tragic execution — it was part of God’s plan to save humanity from sin. Jesus willingly gave up his life as a sacrifice. Before his arrest, Jesus prayed: “Not my will, but yours be done” (Luke 22:42), showing he accepted his suffering as the Father’s will.

Key Fact

Christians believe Jesus’s death on the cross paid the price for human sin. Because Jesus was sinless, his death was a perfect sacrifice that restored the relationship between God and humanity. This is why the cross is the most important symbol in Christianity.

The Resurrection

The resurrection is the belief that Jesus rose from the dead three days after his crucifixion. On Easter Sunday, women visiting Jesus’s tomb found it empty. An angel told them: “He is not here; he has risen!” (Matthew 28:6). Jesus then appeared to his disciples over 40 days.

The resurrection is the most important event in Christianity. St Paul wrote: “If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile” (1 Corinthians 15:17). Without the resurrection, Christianity falls apart.

It proves Jesus is the Son of God. Only God could conquer death. The resurrection confirms that Jesus truly was divine.

It shows God’s power over death. Death is not the end — God has the power to raise the dead. This gives Christians hope that they too will be resurrected.

It confirms the promise of eternal life. Jesus said: “I am the resurrection and the life. The one who believes in me will live, even though they die” (John 11:25).

It is the basis of Christian worship. Christians worship on Sunday because it is the day Jesus rose. Easter is the most important festival in the Christian calendar.

The Ascension

Forty days after the resurrection, Jesus ascended (went up) to heaven. Acts 1:9 describes how “he was taken up before their very eyes, and a cloud hid him from their sight.” Two angels then told the disciples that Jesus would return in the same way.

The ascension is significant because it shows Jesus’s mission on Earth was complete. He returned to the Father, where Christians believe he sits “at the right hand of God” (the Nicene Creed) — a position of honour and authority. The ascension also prepared the way for the Holy Spirit to come at Pentecost, empowering the disciples to spread the Christian message. Christians believe Jesus will return from heaven at the end of time to judge the living and the dead.

Key Fact

The events of Jesus’s life form a connected sequence: the incarnation (God becomes human), the crucifixion (Jesus dies for sin), the resurrection (Jesus conquers death), and the ascension (Jesus returns to heaven). Each event is essential to the Christian understanding of salvation.

title: Pilgrimage & Festivals
content_html:
What Is Pilgrimage?

A pilgrimage is a journey to a place of special religious significance. Christians go on pilgrimages to deepen their faith, seek healing, do penance, experience God in a special way, or feel a connection to important events in Christian history. Some Christians believe that visiting a sacred place brings them closer to God. Others see the journey itself as a spiritual act — a time for prayer, reflection and personal growth.

Not all Christians agree that pilgrimage is necessary. Some argue that God is everywhere and can be worshipped anywhere. Others believe the money spent on travel could be better used to help the poor. However, many Christians value pilgrimage as a powerful expression of faith that has been practised since the earliest centuries of Christianity.

Key Fact

You need to know two contrasting examples of Christian pilgrimage: Lourdes (Roman Catholic, focus on healing) and Iona (ecumenical, focus on community and simplicity). Be ready to explain why Christians visit each and how they differ.

Lourdes

Lourdes is a town in south-west France. In 1858, a 14-year-old girl named Bernadette Soubirous reported 18 visions of the Virgin Mary in a grotto near the river. During one vision, Mary told Bernadette to dig in the ground, and a spring of water appeared. This water is believed by many Catholics to have miraculous healing properties.

Today, around six million pilgrims visit Lourdes each year, making it one of the most visited Christian pilgrimage sites in the world. Pilgrims bathe in or drink the spring water, hoping for physical or spiritual healing. The site includes the Grotto of Massabielle (where the visions occurred), the Basilica of the Immaculate Conception, and hospitals and care facilities for the sick. Over 70 miraculous cures have been officially recognised by the Catholic Church.

Christians visit Lourdes to seek physical healing by bathing in or drinking the spring water. They also go to seek spiritual renewal and forgiveness through prayer and confession. Many go to pray for others who are sick, to feel closer to God in a place associated with the Virgin Mary, or to serve as volunteers caring for the sick and disabled. The sense of community at Lourdes — with millions of believers gathering together — strengthens faith and provides support for those who are suffering.

Iona

Iona is a small island off the west coast of Scotland. In 563 CE, an Irish monk named St Columba founded a monastery there, which became a centre for spreading Christianity across Scotland and northern England. Today, the Iona Community is an ecumenical Christian community that welcomes people of all denominations and none.

Pilgrims visit Iona for its simplicity, peace and sense of spiritual renewal. The community emphasises justice, peace and the integrity of creation. Visitors share in communal worship, manual work and discussion. Unlike Lourdes, Iona does not focus on miracles or healing — instead, it offers a retreat from modern life and an opportunity to live in a simple, prayerful community.

Christmas

Christmas celebrates the Incarnation — the belief that God became human in the person of Jesus Christ. Christians celebrate Christmas on 25 December (though Orthodox Christians celebrate on 7 January). The festival recalls the birth of Jesus in Bethlehem, as described in the Gospels of Matthew and Luke.

Christmas is important because it marks the moment God entered the world as a human being to save humanity from sin. The angel told the shepherds, “Today in the town of David a Saviour has been born to you; he is the Messiah, the Lord” (Luke 2:11). Christians celebrate through special church services (including Midnight Mass and carol services), nativity plays, gift-giving (symbolising the gifts of the Magi) and acts of charity.

For Christians in Great Britain today, Christmas remains the most widely celebrated religious festival. It brings families and communities together. Churches hold special services, including Advent services in the weeks leading up to Christmas, Midnight Mass on Christmas Eve, and Christmas Day worship. Many Christians also see it as a time to help those in need — through charity appeals, food drives and volunteering.

Some Christians are concerned that the religious meaning of Christmas has been overshadowed by commercialism and consumerism. They argue that the focus should be on Jesus’s birth and its theological significance, not on shopping and materialism.

Easter

Easter is the most important festival in the Christian calendar. It celebrates the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, three days after his crucifixion. The events of Easter are central to the Christian faith: without the resurrection, there would be no Christianity. St Paul wrote, “If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile” (1 Corinthians 15:17).

Palm Sunday remembers Jesus’s triumphal entry into Jerusalem, when crowds waved palm branches and shouted “Hosanna!” Maundy Thursday recalls the Last Supper, when Jesus washed his disciples’ feet and shared bread and wine. Good Friday marks the crucifixion and death of Jesus — many churches hold sombre services, and some Christians fast or walk the Stations of the Cross. Easter Sunday celebrates the resurrection — churches hold joyful services with hymns, flowers and the lighting of the Paschal candle.

Key Fact

Easter is the most important Christian festival because it celebrates the resurrection — the foundation of the entire Christian faith. St Paul wrote, “If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile” (1 Corinthians 15:17). Without the resurrection, Christians believe there would be no hope of salvation or eternal life.

title: Life After Death and the Seven Sacraments
content_html:
What Happens After Death?

Catholic Christianity teaches that death is not the end of the human person. Because Jesus rose from the dead on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3–4), Catholics believe that all human beings will one day share in a resurrection of the body. The Nicene Creed declares: “We look for the resurrection of the dead, and the life of the world to come.” This is not a vague idea of the soul floating away — Catholic teaching insists that the whole person, body and soul, will be raised.

After death, Catholic teaching describes a process involving personal judgement, then either heaven, hell or purgatory, followed at the end of time by a final or “Last” Judgement. The Catechism summarises: each person receives a retribution of their souls in the particular judgement immediately after death. The Last Judgement at the end of time will confirm this verdict before all people and before the whole of creation.

Key Fact

Four key elements of Catholic belief about life after death: (1) Resurrection — the whole person (body and soul) will be raised; (2) Judgement — a personal judgement immediately after death and a Last Judgement at the end of time; (3) Heaven — eternal life with God; (4) Purgatory — a process of purification before heaven; Hell is the consequence of a definitive rejection of God’s love.

Heaven, Hell and Purgatory

Heaven is the Catholic term for the perfect communion with God. It is not primarily a physical place but a state of being — the beatific vision, the experience of knowing God directly and fully. Jesus promises: “In my Father’s house are many rooms” (John 14:2). Heaven is the fulfilment of the deepest human longing and the goal of all grace and sacramental life.

Hell is the state of permanent separation from God. Catholic teaching insists that hell is real and that it is the result of a person’s own free choice to reject God definitively. Jesus himself speaks of hell in the Gospels (e.g. Matthew 25:41). The Church does not name any individual as being in hell, and Pope John Paul II emphasised that hell is not so much a punishment imposed by God as a consequence that persons bring on themselves by their choices.

Purgatory is a distinctively Catholic teaching (not held by most Protestant Christians). It refers to a process of purification for those who die in a state of grace but have not yet fully shed their attachment to sin. The Catholic Catechism teaches that those in purgatory are certainly saved — purgatory is not a second chance at salvation — but they undergo a process that prepares them for the full joy of heaven. Catholics pray for those in purgatory, particularly on the feast of All Souls (2 November).

Most Protestant denominations reject the doctrine of purgatory, arguing that it has no clear basis in the Bible and that Christ’s atoning death is fully sufficient — no further purification is needed after death. Protestants generally teach that at death, the saved enter immediately into the presence of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:8: “to be away from the body and at home with the Lord”). Prayers for the dead are not a feature of most Protestant practice.

Eastern Orthodox Christianity shares much Catholic teaching about life after death — resurrection, judgement, heaven and a form of continued development toward God after death — but uses different terminology, speaking of “the toll houses” rather than purgatory, and understands the process through the lens of deification (theosis) rather than legal purification. Orthodox Christians also pray for the dead.

What Is a Sacrament?

The word sacrament comes from the Latin sacramentum, meaning a solemn pledge or sacred action. For Catholics, a sacrament is an outward, physical sign that was instituted by Christ and through which God communicates grace. The physical actions — water poured, oil anointed, bread and wine consecrated — are not mere symbols. They actually convey what they signify. Catholic theology speaks of the “sacramental nature of reality”: the material world is capable of mediating the divine.

There are seven sacraments in Catholic teaching, divided into three groups: sacraments of initiation (Baptism, Confirmation, Eucharist), sacraments of healing (Reconciliation, Anointing of the Sick), and sacraments of service (Holy Orders, Matrimony). The Eucharist holds the supreme place: Catholic teaching describes it as “the source and summit of Christian life” — all other sacraments and all Christian activity flows from and leads back to the Mass.

Key Fact

The seven sacraments: Baptism (removes original sin, initiates into the Church), Confirmation (strengthens faith, gifts of the Holy Spirit), Eucharist (source and summit of Christian life; real presence of Christ), Reconciliation (forgiveness of sin), Anointing of the Sick (healing and comfort in illness), Holy Orders (ordination of deacons, priests and bishops), Matrimony (marriage as a lifelong covenant).

The Eucharist: Source and Summit

The Eucharist (the Mass) holds a unique place among the seven sacraments. Catholic teaching holds the doctrine of transubstantiation: at the consecration, the substance of the bread and wine is changed into the body and blood of Christ, even though the outward appearances (taste, texture) remain. This was formally defined at the Fourth Lateran Council (1215) and reaffirmed at the Council of Trent (1551). The scriptural basis is the Last Supper (Matthew 26:26–28; Luke 22:19–20) and John 6:51: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven.”

Most Protestant Christians do not hold the doctrine of transubstantiation. Many regard the Eucharist as a memorial or symbolic act of remembrance (as Zwingli, a sixteenth-century Swiss reformer, taught) rather than an actual change in the elements. Some Protestant traditions (notably Lutheran) hold a doctrine of “real presence” that does not go as far as transubstantiation. Eastern Orthodox Christianity teaches that Christ is truly present in the Eucharist but has not adopted the specific philosophical language of transubstantiation. For Catholics, this difference about the Eucharist is one of the most significant points of divergence among Christian traditions.

Baptism is the first and foundational sacrament. Catholic teaching holds that all human beings are born with original sin — the consequence of the first human disobedience described in Genesis 3 — which creates a barrier between humanity and God. Baptism, in which water is poured three times in the name of the Trinity, removes original sin and initiates the person into the Church. It is the door to all the other sacraments.

Most Protestant traditions also practise baptism but differ on its effects. Some (e.g. Baptist, evangelical) insist baptism must be chosen by a believing adult (believer’s baptism) and regard it as an outward sign of inward faith rather than a sacrament that confers grace. Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican traditions generally baptise infants, believing that baptism itself communicates grace and removes original sin regardless of the recipient’s age or choice.

title: Mission, Evangelism & the Worldwide Church
content_html:
The Church in the Local Community

The Church is not just a building — it is the community of believers who follow Jesus’s teachings. Christians believe they have a duty to help others in their local area. Jesus taught, “Love your neighbour as yourself” (Mark 12:31), and the Parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:25–37) shows that ‘neighbour’ means anyone in need, regardless of background.

Many churches are active in their communities, running projects that support vulnerable people. Two important examples of local church action are food banks and street pastors.

Key Fact

You need to know about the Church’s role in the local community, including food banks and street pastors. These are practical examples of Christians putting Jesus’s teaching about loving your neighbour into action.

Food Banks

Food banks collect donated food and distribute it to people in crisis — those who cannot afford to feed themselves or their families. The Trussell Trust, founded on Christian principles, runs over 1,400 food bank centres across the UK. People are referred to food banks by professionals such as doctors, social workers or schools, and receive an emergency food parcel lasting three days.

Christians support food banks because Jesus taught that helping others is the same as serving God: “For I was hungry and you gave me something to eat” (Matthew 25:35). Churches provide volunteers, collection points and premises for food banks, putting their faith into practical action.

Street Pastors

Street pastors are trained Christian volunteers who patrol town and city centres at night, usually on Friday and Saturday evenings. They care for vulnerable people — offering water, flip-flops to those in bare feet, warm clothing, and a listening ear. They help people who are drunk, distressed or at risk of harm, and liaise with police and ambulance services when needed.

The Street Pastors movement was founded in London in 2003 by Reverend Les Isaac. It now operates in over 300 locations across the UK. Street pastors do not preach or try to convert people — they simply demonstrate Christian love through practical care. Their presence has been shown to reduce crime and antisocial behaviour in many areas.

Mission is the broader calling of the Church to carry out God’s work in the world. This includes preaching the gospel, caring for the poor, promoting justice and working for peace. Evangelism is the specific act of spreading the Christian faith — sharing the good news of Jesus Christ with non-believers.

Jesus commanded his followers to evangelise: “Go and make disciples of all nations, baptising them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19). This is known as the Great Commission. Christians carry out evangelism in many ways — through preaching, missionary work overseas, Alpha courses, social media and personal example. Church growth depends on both evangelism (reaching new people) and nurturing existing believers.

The Worldwide Church

The Church operates on a global scale. Christians believe they have a responsibility not just to their local community but to the whole world. The worldwide Church works for reconciliation (bringing peace between conflicting groups), responds to persecution, and addresses global poverty and injustice.

Reconciliation is central to Christian teaching. Jesus said, “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God” (Matthew 5:9). The worldwide Church works to bring peace in areas of conflict — for example, the role of churches in the peace process in Northern Ireland and in post-apartheid South Africa, where Archbishop Desmond Tutu led the Truth and Reconciliation Commission.

Many Christians around the world face persecution for their faith. In some countries, Christians are imprisoned, attacked or even killed for practising their religion. Churches respond by praying for persecuted Christians, raising awareness, campaigning for religious freedom and providing practical support. Jesus warned his followers that persecution would come: “If they persecuted me, they will persecute you also” (John 15:20).

CAFOD (Catholic Agency For Overseas Development) is the official Catholic aid agency for England and Wales. It works in over 40 countries, providing emergency relief after disasters, funding long-term development projects (clean water, education, healthcare) and campaigning for justice. CAFOD is funded mainly by Catholic parishes.

Christian Aid works with communities of all faiths and none in around 37 countries. It tackles poverty through emergency response, long-term development and advocacy for policy change. Christian Aid Week, held every May, raises millions of pounds through door-to-door collections and fundraising events across UK churches.

Tearfund is an evangelical Christian charity that works in over 50 countries. It partners with local churches to address poverty, provide disaster relief, and support communities in building sustainable livelihoods. Tearfund’s distinctive approach is to work through local church networks, believing that churches are uniquely placed to understand and serve their communities.

All three organisations are motivated by Jesus’s teaching to love your neighbour and care for the poor. Jesus said, “Whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers and sisters of mine, you did for me” (Matthew 25:40).

Key Fact

The specification requires knowledge of the work of one of CAFOD, Christian Aid or Tearfund. All three are motivated by Jesus’s teaching to love your neighbour (Mark 12:31) and serve the poor (Matthew 25:40), but they differ in their denominational links and methods.

title: The Trinity and the Nicene Creed
content_html:
One God, Three Persons

At the heart of Catholic Christianity is the belief that God is the Trinity — one God who exists as three co-equal and co-eternal persons: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. This is not a belief in three separate gods. Catholic teaching insists firmly on the oneness of God alongside the three-ness of persons. The Nicene Creed opens with the declaration “We believe in one God” before naming the three persons in turn.

A common misconception is that Christians — and Catholics in particular — believe in three gods. The technical phrase that earns marks in an exam is “one God, three persons” or, in the language of the early Church, “one substance, three persons” (from the Latin una substantia, tres personae). Each person is distinct but not separate: the Father is not the Son, the Son is not the Holy Spirit, yet all three are fully God.

Key Fact

The Trinity: God the Father is the creator and sustainer of all things; God the Son (Jesus Christ) is the incarnate Word who redeems humanity; God the Holy Spirit is the presence of God active in the world and in believers today. One God, three persons — this is the foundational Catholic belief.

Scriptural Origins of the Trinity

The doctrine of the Trinity is rooted in scripture. At the baptism of Jesus, all three persons are present simultaneously: Jesus is baptised in the River Jordan, the Holy Spirit descends on him “like a dove”, and the voice of the Father speaks from heaven: “This is my Son, whom I love; with him I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:16–17). The Great Commission in Matthew 28:19 instructs the disciples to baptise “in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” — a single name held by three persons.

The Gospel of John deepens the Trinitarian picture. John 1:1 declares: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” This Logos (Word) was present at creation and became flesh in Jesus (John 1:14). Paul’s letters develop the idea of the Spirit dwelling in believers (Romans 8:9–11), completing the Trinitarian picture that the Church would later formalise.

By the early fourth century, debate had erupted within the Church about the exact relationship between the Father and the Son. A theologian called Arius argued that the Son was a created being — subordinate to the Father and not fully divine. This was widely held to be a serious error by the majority of bishops. Emperor Constantine convened the first ecumenical council at Nicaea in modern-day Turkey in 325 CE to settle the dispute.

The council condemned Arianism and produced the Nicene Creed — a formal statement of orthodox belief. The creed declares that the Son is “of one substance with the Father” (the Greek word homoousios), directly contradicting Arius. The creed was later refined at the Council of Constantinople (381 CE) to include a fuller statement on the Holy Spirit, reaching the form Catholics recite at Mass today.

The Three Persons and Their Roles

Catholic theology distinguishes the persons of the Trinity by their roles in relation to humanity. God the Father is the creator of heaven and earth. The Nicene Creed begins: “I believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth, of all things visible and invisible.” The Father is the source and origin of all being, though always in relation to the Son and the Spirit.

God the Son is the eternal Word who took on human flesh — the incarnation. The creed describes him as “God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, of one substance with the Father.” The Son’s role is the redemption of humanity through his life, death and resurrection. The Holy Spirit is the Lord and giver of life, proceeding from the Father and (in Western Catholic teaching) from the Son also — the filioque clause that distinguishes Catholic from Eastern Orthodox theology.

All three major Christian traditions — Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant — affirm the Trinity as expressed in the Nicene Creed, so there is broad agreement on the core doctrine. The differences lie in emphasis and specific theological formulations.

Eastern Orthodox Christianity rejects the filioque addition (the teaching that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son), which was inserted by the Western Church in the early medieval period. Orthodox theologians argue this addition distorts the balance between the three persons. Protestant Christianity shares the Nicene definition of the Trinity but may place greater emphasis on scripture as the primary source of Trinitarian knowledge, whereas Catholic theology gives significant weight to Church tradition and the Magisterium (the Church’s teaching authority) in interpreting the doctrine.

The Trinity in Catholic Life Today

The Trinity is not merely an abstract theological formula in Catholic life — it shapes daily practice. Catholics begin and end prayer with the Sign of the Cross: “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” The Mass opens and closes with Trinitarian language. Baptism is performed “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19), bringing the new Christian into relationship with all three persons. The Magisterium — the Church’s official teaching body — holds that the Trinitarian faith cannot be separated from Christian life: to know God is to know him as Father, Son and Spirit.

In parishes across Britain today, the Nicene Creed is recited aloud by the whole congregation at Mass every Sunday. For many Catholics at Westminster Cathedral in London or at their local parish church, the creed is not experienced as doctrine alone but as a communal act of worship — a shared declaration of who God is and who the believer is in relation to God.

Key Fact

The Nicene Creed (325 CE, refined 381 CE) is the definitive Catholic statement of Trinitarian belief. It declares the Son is “of one substance with the Father” (homoousios) — directly countering the Arian view that the Son was a created being. Catholics recite the Nicene Creed at every Mass.

title: Sacraments: Baptism & Holy Communion
content_html:
What Is a Sacrament?

A sacrament is a sacred ritual through which Christians believe they receive God’s grace. The word comes from the Latin ‘sacramentum’, meaning a solemn oath. Sacraments are outward, visible signs of an inward, spiritual blessing. Roman Catholic and Orthodox Christians recognise seven sacraments, while most Protestant churches recognise only two — baptism and Holy Communion. These two were specifically commanded by Jesus in the Gospels.

Key Fact

A sacrament is an outward sign of inward grace. Roman Catholics recognise seven sacraments, while most Protestants recognise only two — baptism and Holy Communion — because only these were directly instituted by Jesus.

Infant Baptism

Infant baptism is practised by Roman Catholic, Anglican and Methodist churches. During the ceremony, a priest or minister pours water over the baby’s head three times in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Parents and godparents make promises on the child’s behalf to reject evil and turn to Christ.

For Catholics, infant baptism removes original sin — the sinful state inherited from Adam and Eve. The baby receives a white garment symbolising purity and a candle symbolising the light of Christ. Other Christians see it as a way of welcoming the child into the Church community and dedicating them to God. Jesus himself said, “Let the little children come to me, and do not hinder them” (Mark 10:14).

Believers’ baptism is practised by Baptist and Pentecostal churches. It involves the full immersion of a person who is old enough to make their own declaration of faith. The person is submerged completely under water and then raised up — symbolising dying to their old sinful life and being raised to new life in Christ, mirroring Jesus’s death and resurrection.

Baptists argue that babies cannot understand the commitment being made. They point to the example of Jesus, who was baptised as an adult by John the Baptist in the River Jordan (Matthew 3:13–17). Believers’ baptism is a personal choice and a public declaration of faith, making the commitment more meaningful.

Different Beliefs About Baptism

Christians hold different views on which form of baptism is correct. Those who practise infant baptism believe that God’s grace should be available to everyone from birth and that parents can make promises on a child’s behalf. Those who practise believers’ baptism argue that faith requires a conscious, personal decision and that Jesus was baptised as an adult. Some Christians, such as the Salvation Army and Quakers, do not practise baptism at all — they believe the inward spiritual change matters more than the outward ritual.

Key Fact

Infant baptism and believers’ baptism share the same purpose — entry into the Christian faith — but differ in method and timing. Infant baptism uses pouring of water and relies on parents’ promises; believers’ baptism uses full immersion and requires a personal declaration of faith.

Holy Communion / The Eucharist

Holy Communion (also called the Eucharist, the Lord’s Supper or the Mass) remembers the Last Supper, the final meal Jesus shared with his disciples before his crucifixion. At this meal, Jesus took bread and said, “This is my body given for you; do this in remembrance of me,” and took wine saying, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood” (Luke 22:19–20).

In the Roman Catholic Church, the Mass is the central act of worship. Catholics believe in transubstantiation — that the bread and wine literally become the body and blood of Christ during the service. Only a priest can celebrate Mass, and the service follows a strict liturgical structure.

In Orthodox churches, the Divine Liturgy is a highly elaborate and symbolic celebration. The bread and wine are also believed to become the body and blood of Christ, though the Orthodox Church does not use the term transubstantiation.

In Protestant churches, Holy Communion is generally seen as a symbolic act of remembrance rather than a literal transformation. Anglicans vary in their interpretation — some lean towards the Catholic view, others see it as symbolic. Methodists and Baptists see the bread and wine as symbols of Jesus’s body and blood, taken in remembrance of his sacrifice.

The Salvation Army and Quakers do not celebrate Holy Communion. They believe that the spiritual reality of Christ’s presence does not depend on physical elements and that every meal can be sacred.

Holy Communion is important to Christians for several reasons. It obeys Jesus’s direct command to “do this in remembrance of me.” It brings Christians closer to God and to one another through a shared sacred meal. It reminds believers of Jesus’s sacrifice on the cross and the promise of salvation. For Catholics, receiving the Eucharist is considered essential for spiritual nourishment — Jesus said, “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you” (John 6:53).

Key Fact

The biggest difference in Holy Communion is between Catholics, who believe the bread and wine literally become the body and blood of Christ (transubstantiation), and most Protestants, who see it as a symbolic remembrance of Jesus’s sacrifice at the Last Supper.

title: The Nature of God & the Trinity
content_html:
The Nature of God

Christians are monotheistic — they believe in one God who created and sustains everything. Although God is called “Father,” Christians do not believe God has a physical body or a gender. God is a spirit, beyond human understanding, and is considered holy — completely pure, set apart and worthy of worship.

The Nicene Creed, recited by Christians worldwide, opens with the words: “We believe in One God.” Christians believe this one God has several key qualities that together make God perfect. Three of these qualities are central to the AQA specification: God as omnipotent, God as loving (benevolent), and God as just.

God as Omnipotent

Omnipotent means all-powerful. Christians believe God has unlimited power and authority — nothing is beyond what God can do. God demonstrated this power by creating the entire universe from nothing and continues to sustain all life.

Key Fact

“Nothing is impossible with God.” (Luke 1:37) — These words were spoken by the Angel Gabriel to the Virgin Mary. Christians use this verse to show that God’s power has absolutely no limits.

Belief in God’s omnipotence influences Christians in several ways. When they see the complexity of nature, they see evidence of a powerful creator. It also means they trust that God can perform miracles, and it gives them confidence when they pray that God has the power to answer.

God as Loving (Benevolent)

Benevolent means all-loving and all-good. Christians believe God loves every human being unconditionally. God created humans out of love and wants to share that love with all creation.

Key Fact

“God so loved the world that he gave his one and only Son, that whoever believes in him shall not perish but have eternal life.” (John 3:16) — Christians see sending Jesus as the greatest act of God’s love.

This belief helps Christians feel valued and gives them a purpose — to share God’s love with others through kindness, charity and forgiveness. Because God is all-loving, Christians believe God forgives those who are truly sorry for their sins.

God as Just

Christians believe God is a just (fair) judge of all humanity. Because God is all-powerful and all-loving, God is the perfect giver of justice. This means God will never support injustice, oppression, prejudice or cruelty.

“God is just: He will pay back trouble to those who trouble you.” (2 Thessalonians 1:6) — This teaches Christians that God sees all actions and will judge everyone fairly. No wrongdoing will go unnoticed. Because of this, Christians are motivated to fight against injustice wherever they encounter it.

The Problem of Evil and Suffering

If God is omnipotent, loving and just, why does evil and suffering exist? This is called the problem of evil, and it is one of the biggest challenges to Christian belief.

The problem can be stated simply: if God is loving, he would want to stop suffering; if God is powerful, he could stop suffering; if God is just, he would not allow injustice. Yet suffering clearly exists. The philosopher David Hume called this the “inconsistent triad” — the three ideas seem to contradict each other.

Christians distinguish between two types of evil. Moral evil is caused by human actions — murder, theft, war and cruelty. Natural evil is caused by the natural world — earthquakes, disease, floods and famine.

Free will: God gave humans the freedom to choose how to live. Some choose to do wrong, causing moral evil. Christians argue that genuine free will is better than being puppets, even if some misuse it.

Life as a test: Some Christians believe suffering tests faith. The story of Job shows that God allows suffering to test whether people remain faithful — and rewards those who do.

Part of God’s plan: Humans cannot fully understand God’s reasons. “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you” (Jeremiah 1:5) suggests God has a purpose for every person, even if suffering seems unfair.

The Devil: Some Christians believe Satan tempts people into sin. Evil is caused by the Devil, not by God — though this raises the question of why God allows the Devil to operate.

The Oneness of God and the Trinity

Although Christians believe in one God, they understand God as existing in three persons: Father, Son (Jesus Christ) and Holy Spirit. This is called the Trinity. It does not mean there are three separate gods — the three persons are all fully God, sharing one divine nature.

Key Fact

The Trinity is one God in three persons: the Father (creator and sustainer), the Son (Jesus Christ, who became human to save humanity), and the Holy Spirit (God’s presence active in the world today). All three are equal and eternal.

God the Father is the creator and sustainer of all life. He is the source of all things and the one to whom Christians direct their prayers. Jesus taught his followers to pray “Our Father.”

God the Son is Jesus Christ. Christians believe the Son has always existed with the Father but took human form (the incarnation) to live among people, teach them about God, and die on the cross to save humanity from sin.

God the Holy Spirit is the unseen power of God at work in the world. Christians believe the Holy Spirit guides, comforts and strengthens believers. At Pentecost, the Holy Spirit descended on the disciples as tongues of fire (Acts 2), empowering them to spread the Christian message.

The Nicene Creed affirms the Trinity: “We believe in one God, the Father Almighty… And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God… And in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and Giver of Life.” The Trinity is central to Christian worship — Christians are baptised “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19).

Some Christians find the Trinity difficult to understand. Common analogies include water existing as ice, liquid and steam (three forms, one substance), or the sun giving light, heat and energy. However, these analogies are imperfect — the Trinity is considered a mystery that humans can only partly grasp.
